# 5. Results and discussion

This section reports what the matched meta-stochastic frontier reveals about crop production in households that used credit relative to matched households that did not, and interprets the estimates against the hypotheses of Section 4.1 and the financing environment of Section 3. Section 5.1 presents the diagnostics that justify the frontier specification and the separation of the two groups' technologies. Section 5.2 compares input elasticities and returns to scale across the naive, group and metafrontiers, which speaks to H3. Section 5.3 carries the paper's central result, the decomposition of the credit contrast into a technology gap and a technical-efficiency gap, together with what matching changes and what the matched input and output gaps of Figure 1 add. Because the central result runs against H1, Section 5.4 weighs the readings of it that the data can and cannot support. Section 5.5 tests whether the decomposition survives alternative treatment definitions, matched samples and frontier specifications, and Section 5.6 asks for whom, for which crops and where the gaps are concentrated. Unless stated otherwise, estimates refer to the household credit definition on the one-to-one matched sample, a translog frontier with a half-normal inefficiency term and the regularity restrictions imposed, with jackknife standard errors from 100 delete-one-enumeration-area replicates. Every difference is reported as credit users less non-users, and every difference is an association conditional on observables in a balanced sample, in the sense set out in Section 4.4.

## 5.1 Diagnostic tests

Table 4 reports the diagnostics for the five frontiers estimated: the naive national frontier, the two group frontiers for non-users [A] and credit users [B], and the metafrontier on the matched and unmatched samples. The first question is whether a one-sided inefficiency component belongs in the error at all. The residual-skewness statistics of @Schmidt1984 and @Coelli1995 are negative for every frontier, as a one-sided term in a production frontier implies, the Coelli statistic ranging from `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Coelli (1995)", 3), 2)` for the credit-user frontier to `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Coelli (1995)", 6), 2)` for the unmatched metafrontier, and the boundary likelihood-ratio test of @Gutierrez2001 rejects the null of no inefficiency in each case, with statistics of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 2), 1)` and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 3), 1)` for the non-user and credit-user frontiers and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Gutierrez (2001)", 5), 1)` for the matched metafrontier. Deviations from the frontier are therefore not attributable to symmetric noise alone, and a stochastic frontier rather than an average-response production function is the appropriate description of the data.

The second question is whether credit users and non-users can be assessed against a single frontier. The metafrontier likelihood-ratio test rejects a common technology in both samples, with statistics of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Meta frontier LR test", 5), 0)` on the matched sample and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Meta frontier LR test", 6), 0)` on the unmatched sample, far above any conventional critical value. The two groups produce under different technologies, so their performance has to be decomposed into how well each group uses its own technology and how far that technology sits from best practice, which is what Equations (4) and (5) do; comparing the groups through a single pooled efficiency score would conflate the two, which is the confounding that metafrontier applications to Ghanaian agriculture have been designed to avoid [@Ansah2023a; @Adaku2023; @Asravor2024; @Tsiboe2021a].

The third set of diagnostics concerns regularity and the composition of the error. At the observation level the single frontiers are only partly well behaved: monotonicity holds for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 1, 0)` of observations under the naive frontier and for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 2, 0)` and `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 3, 0)` under the non-user and credit-user frontiers, and curvature for only `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 1, 0)`, `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 2, 0)` and `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 3, 0)` respectively, although every elasticity is positive at the sample means at which it is evaluated, so the models are well behaved on average even where individual observations violate the conditions. The regularity-restricted metafrontier does what it is meant to do: monotonicity is satisfied for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Monotonicity satisfaction rate", 5, 0)` of observations in both the matched and the unmatched metafrontier, and curvature for `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 5, 0)` of observations in the matched metafrontier against `r tbl_pct("table4", "Curvature satisfaction rate", 6, 0)` in the unmatched one. The matched metafrontier is therefore the specification on which the elasticities and technology gaps below can be read with the least concern about local violations of economic regularity, which is one reason, alongside covariate balance, for treating the matched estimates as the preferred ones. The share of composed-error variance attributable to the one-sided term, $\gamma = \sigma_{u}^{2}/\sigma^{2}$, is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 2), 3)` in the non-user frontier and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 3), 3)` in the credit-user frontier, so within each group the dominant source of unexplained dispersion is inefficiency rather than noise; in the metafrontier, where the one-sided term is the technology gap, the share is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 5), 3)` on the matched sample against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Ratio variance due to inefficiency", 6), 3)` on the unmatched one, so most of the distance between the group frontiers and the envelope is systematic rather than idiosyncratic. Both margins matter, which is the premise on which the metafrontier design rests.

## 5.2 Output elasticities and returns to scale

Table 4 reports input elasticities evaluated at the sample means, with the underlying translog coefficients in Table S3. Under the naive national frontier every input has a positive elasticity that is significant at the 1% level, consistent with earlier frontier estimates for Ghanaian crop production on these data [@Tsiboe2021a; @Ansah2023a; @Adaku2023; @Asravor2024]. Land dominates, with an elasticity of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 1), 3)`, followed by family labour (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 1), 3)`), planting material (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 1), 3)`), pesticide (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 1), 3)`), hired labour (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Hired labour", 1), 3)`) and fertilizer (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 1), 3)`). Returns to scale are `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 1), 3)`, marginally above constant. The ordering is the familiar one for Ghanaian smallholders, whose output responds overwhelmingly to the extensive margin and to household labour and only modestly to purchased inputs.

The group frontiers speak to H3, and they bear it out in one dimension and contradict it in the other. Because the jackknife standard errors are small, every difference in the [B−A] column is statistically significant, so magnitude carries the economic content, and on that criterion one input dominates the table. The land elasticity is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 3), 3)` for credit users against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 2), 3)` for non-users, a difference of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 4), 3)` that is roughly a ninth of the non-user elasticity and accounts for essentially the whole of the returns-to-scale gap (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 3), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 2), 3)`, a difference of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 4), 3)`). No other input moves by as much as a hundredth of output. Family labour is slightly lower for credit users (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 3), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 2), 3)`), as are hired labour and planting material; fertilizer and pesticide are slightly higher. H3 anticipated that credit would raise the response to land and to labour more than the response to fertilizer. The land half is borne out emphatically. The labour half is not: both labour elasticities move against credit users, and the fertilizer elasticity rises rather than holding flat, by `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 4), 3)` on a non-user base of `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Fertilizer", 2), 3)` — proportionally the largest movement in the table, though far too small in absolute terms to reorder the inputs within either group. The credit-user technology is therefore not more input-responsive across the board, and it is not the working-capital margins that distinguish it; what distinguishes it is a much stronger output response to land, at mildly increasing rather than slightly decreasing returns to scale.

That fertilizer margin is worth a paragraph of its own, because a leading account of low fertilizer use in African agriculture attributes it to uninsured risk acting together with the absence of credit rather than to either alone: in Ethiopia, households more exposed to a shortfall in consumption after a bad harvest applied less fertilizer, so that risk and the inability to borrow against the outlay reinforced one another [@Dercon2011]. If that account carried over to the population studied here, households whose credit constraint is the less binding of the two should show a distinctly different fertilizer regime from comparable non-borrowers. They show the opposite of one. Borrowing households apply about a tenth less fertilizer per hectare than their matched comparators, as Section 5.3 sets out, and their frontier is more responsive to fertilizer at the margin, not less. Those two facts fit together, but not in the way a relaxed credit constraint would predict: a farm applying less of an input sits farther up its own response curve, so a higher marginal product is what one expects of a group that uses less fertilizer, not evidence that finance has loosened the fertilizer margin. The Ethiopian evidence therefore stands as a contrast to what these data show rather than a confirmation of it, and the contrast is one more reason to ask, as Section 5.4 does, whether the borrowing recorded here is the kind that finances fertilizer at all.

Two readings of the land result are consistent with the data, and the design cannot separate them. One is that credit-using households are operating where area is the binding factor, so that additional land still adds substantially to output; an elasticity describes the curvature of a group's frontier at its mean input bundle, and a high land elasticity is what a frontier looks like at a point where the complementary inputs are thin — which, as Figure 1 shows below, is exactly where these farms sit, applying less of every purchased input per hectare than their matched comparators. The other is compositional: the group frontier is fitted on the borrowing households as they are, and a frontier fitted on a group that differs in farm size, tenure or agro-ecology can display a higher land elasticity without any change in how a given household farms. The returns-to-scale contrast sharpens the question rather than settling it. Credit users' frontier shows mildly increasing returns (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 3), 3)`) where non-users' shows slightly decreasing ones (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 2), 3)`), so a proportional expansion of all inputs would raise output more than proportionately for the borrowing group — which is what an unrelieved liquidity constraint looks like from the production side, and which sits pointedly beside the finding of Section 5.3 that the same group operates farther from best practice. Table S3 adds one feature worth carrying forward to the heterogeneity results, and it is a reversal rather than a difference of degree. The coefficient on the cocoa area share is negative in the naive national frontier (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS3", "Cocoa", 1), 3)`) and more strongly negative in the non-user frontier (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS3", "Cocoa", 2), 3)`), but positive and large in the credit-user frontier (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS3", "Cocoa", 3), 3)`), all significant at the 1% level. Under the technology non-users operate, a larger cocoa share is associated with lower output at given inputs; under the technology credit users operate, with higher output. The credit-user technology is therefore favourable to cocoa in a way the comparison group's is not, even though, as shown below, it is less favourable to every other crop.

The last two columns of Table 4 give the metafrontier elasticities on the matched and unmatched samples. The two are close and preserve the same ranking of inputs: land is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 5), 3)` matched against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Land", 6), 3)` unmatched, family labour `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Family labour", 6), 3)`, planting material `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Planting material", 6), 3)`, pesticide `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Pesticide", 6), 3)`, and returns to scale `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 5), 3)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Returns to scale", 6), 3)`, with hired labour and fertilizer coinciding to within a thousandth. Balancing the sample therefore changes the shape of the envelope only modestly; its main effect, shown next, is on the position of the two groups relative to it. What the elasticities establish is that the best-practice technology, like both group technologies, is land-intensive with near-constant returns to scale, so the technology gaps discussed next are gaps in the level of the frontier rather than in its shape.

## 5.3 Technology gaps, technical efficiency and meta-frontier efficiency

Table 4 decomposes performance into the technology gap ratio of Equation (4), pure technical efficiency from Equation (2) and their product, meta-frontier technical efficiency, from Equation (5); the Matched rows are the preferred estimates and the Unmatched rows show what balancing the sample changes. Table 5 repeats the matched comparison for the household definition alongside the narrower definitions of who in the household borrowed, which Section 5.5 takes up.

The technology gap is the headline result, and it runs against H1. In the matched sample the mean TGR is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 3)` for credit users: the technology set operated by non-users produces, on average, `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 0)` of the output attainable under the best-practice technology at the same inputs, and that of credit users `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)"), 0)`. The difference of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points is significant at the 1% level, is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5, and is negative. Section 4.1 hypothesized the opposite on the grounds that credit finances the lumpy investments that move a farm toward best practice. In these data borrowing households are not, as a group, operating the best-practice technology; their frontier lies farther inside the metafrontier than the frontier of comparable non-users, and matching on gender, round, region, agro-ecology, locality and a rich set of household, farm and financial-inclusion covariates does not remove that difference. The unmatched gap is of the same sign and similar size (`r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points), so the finding is not created by matching either.

Pure technical efficiency, which measures each group against its own frontier, differs little between the groups. On the matched sample mean TE is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 3)` for credit users, a difference of `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 1)` percentage points in favour of credit users that is significant at the 1% level and is reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5. What is unstable is not the sign within the matched sample but what happens when the samples are not balanced: unmatched, the same comparison runs `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` percentage points against credit users, and Section 5.5 shows that the sign also moves across the definition of who borrowed and across aggregation rules. Both differences are statistically significant, because the jackknife standard errors are small; but a difference that reverses when the comparison group is rebalanced, and that stays within a few percentage points of zero under every specification examined, is not one on which an interpretation should rest. The defensible statement is that, relative to their own technology, credit users and matched non-users are about equally efficient, each attaining roughly `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)"), 0)` of their own frontier output, a level of within-technology inefficiency in line with earlier Ghanaian frontier studies [@Ansah2023a; @Asravor2024; @Adaku2023]. H2, which predicted lower efficiency among credit users, is not supported: in the balanced comparison the small difference runs the other way, and we do not read these data as establishing an efficiency effect of borrowing in either direction.

Because the efficiency margin is close to neutral, the meta-frontier efficiency gap is the technology gap. Matched MTE is `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` for non-users and `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 3)` for credit users, a statistically significant shortfall of `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` percentage points, reproduced exactly in the first row of Table 5. The MTE gap is negative, significant and of the same order as the TGR gap, so the shortfall of credit-using households relative to best practice is a technology gap and not an efficiency gap. Both groups, it should be stressed, operate well inside the metafrontier, at about `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 2, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 0)` and `r fmt_pct(tbl_num("table4", "Matched", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)"), 0)` of attainable output; the credit gap is a modest increment on a large common shortfall of the kind widely documented for African smallholders [@Ogundari2014; @Ansah2023a], and the economically relevant statement is not that borrowers farm worse but that the technology they farm with is, on average, farther from the best available, by an amount several times the efficiency difference in either direction. The attribution differs from the one @Ansah2023a report across agro-ecologies, where technical inefficiency outweighs technology differences. The two results are not in conflict, because they decompose different contrasts, but together they caution against assuming that any production shortfall in Ghana is a management problem.

The comparison between the matched and unmatched rows of Table 4 shows what matching does to these contrasts, and it is the most informative feature of the table. In the unmatched sample credit users trail non-users by `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` percentage points in TE and `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table4", "Unmatched", 4, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points in MTE, several times the matched values, whereas the unmatched TGR gap is close to the matched one. Balancing the two groups on observables therefore removes almost all of the raw efficiency disadvantage of borrowers and most of the raw MTE deficit, but leaves the technology gap essentially intact. The raw efficiency deficit was compositional, a statement about who borrows on the dimensions Section 4.3 balances; the technology gap survives the comparison of like with like. Observable selection into borrowing explains the efficiency difference and almost none of the technology difference.

Figure 1 places the frontier results beside the input and output levels of the matched pairs. It reports, for the matched sample, the proportional gap associated with credit in each per-hectare input and in the real value of output per hectare, evaluated for the sample as a whole and with reference to the non-user and user subsamples. Credit-using households apply substantially less planting material, hired labour, pesticide and fertilizer per hectare than their matched comparators, the planting-material gap being by some way the largest and each of the four significant at the 1% level; land area, against which the other inputs are normalized, registers no gap; household labour does not differ significantly; and the value of output per hectare is slightly higher for credit users, a difference that does not approach conventional significance. The three reference populations give nearly identical gaps, so the pattern does not depend on which group's covariate distribution is used. Two things follow. First, the hired-labour advantage of borrowing households in the unmatched data of Table 1 (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Hired labour (man-days/ha)", 3), 0)` against `r fmt_num(tbl_num("table1", "Hired labour (man-days/ha)", 2), 0)` man-days per hectare) does not survive comparison with observably similar non-borrowers; it reflected who borrows rather than what borrowing finances. Second, credit is not associated with intensification on the purchased-input margin in these data, which is the opposite of what a liquidity-relaxing account of credit predicts, and the input on which borrowers fall furthest behind is planting material rather than fertilizer, so the shortfall is not confined to the input for which seasonal finance is most often advocated. Read with Table 4, the picture is coherent: a borrowing group whose technology leans heavily on land and thinly on everything bought, whose household labour is neither more plentiful nor more productive at the margin, which lies inside the best-practice envelope, produces about as much per hectare as the comparison group, and is run about as efficiently, relative to that technology, as the comparison group runs its own. The lower TGR of credit users therefore cannot be read as borrowed money buying inputs that fail to raise output; it is the technology in use, evaluated at common input levels, that sits farther from best practice.

## 5.4 Interpreting the negative technology gap

The technology gap is measured against a metafrontier that envelops both group frontiers, so a lower TGR for credit users says that the technology of borrowing households, as a group, is not the best practice in the sample. It does not say what makes it so, and Section 4.4 rules out a causal reading. Four readings are consistent with the evidence of Sections 2, 3 and 5.3, and the data discriminate among them only partially.

The first is loan use. Household credit relaxes the household's liquidity constraint, not the farm's, and the loan-purpose codes of Table 3 show that agriculture is a minority use of it: in 2012/13, the round in which the recorded purposes exhaust the loans, only `r tbl_pct("table3", "Agricultural", 1, 1)` were taken for agricultural purposes, the remainder financing business, education, ceremonies, debt repayment and other household needs. Fungibility of agricultural credit within the household is well documented [@Hussain2016], and Figure 1 is what fungibility looks like on the farm: borrowing households are not the ones applying more purchased inputs. On this reading the negative technology gap is not a failure of credit to reach the farm so much as evidence that, for most of these households, the loan was never directed there, and the household indicator identifies households with a reason to borrow rather than farms with financed technology. This is the reading the exhibits most directly support, and Table 5 adds to it the sharpest evidence the design can offer. Splitting the treatment by who in the household held the loan, the technology gap is widest when the spouse borrowed, intermediate when another member did, and indistinguishable from zero when the operator borrowed on their own account. If the gap were a property of borrowing households as such, it should not vanish in the one case where the borrower and the farmer are the same person; that it does is what a loan-use account predicts, since the operator's own loan is the one with the shortest path to the farm. The reading is also consistent with the northern-Ghana finding that even input-linked credit raised input use without proportionate output gains [@Iddrisu2018]. It remains a reading rather than a result: the survey records the stated purpose of a loan but not the use of each cedi, the operator-only estimate is imprecise as well as small, and the matching balances households on having credit rather than on who holds it, so the four rows compare differently-composed groups.

The second is selection on what the GLSS does not record. Matching balances the covariates in Table 1 and Fig. S1, but not the reasons a household applies for a loan and a lender grants it. Distress borrowing after a shock, borrowing to fund a non-farm enterprise, and lender targeting of households with particular repayment prospects would each place borrowers on a different technology for reasons the design cannot see, and the growing share of group-based microfinance in Table 3, from `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 1, 1)` to `r tbl_pct("table3", "Group based micro-finance or lending", 2, 1)` of loans, means that allocation increasingly runs through community institutions whose membership the GLSS does not observe. Differences in risk preference that affect both borrowing and technology choice belong here too [@Dercon2011]. The stability of the TGR gap between the unmatched and matched samples is consistent with this reading, since it shows that the gap is orthogonal to the observables the matching uses; it cannot show whether the gap is orthogonal to what the matching does not use, and the direction of the resulting bias is not signed. The pattern across borrowers in Table 5 sits awkwardly with a purely selective account, however. Selection on unrecorded farm circumstances should if anything be sharpest where the operator is the borrower, since that is the case in which the decision to borrow is most closely tied to the farm; instead it is the case in which no technology gap appears. That does not rule the reading out -- who within a household borrows is itself a choice, and the operator-only estimate is imprecise -- but a selection story has to explain why the gap is absent exactly where the selection into borrowing should be most farm-specific.

The third is the distinction between use and access. The treatment is an indicator of having borrowed, and the modal reason for not applying is having no need for a loan (`r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 1, 1)` and `r tbl_pct("table3", "No need", 2, 1)` of non-applicants in the two rounds, Table 3), so the comparison group mixes households that are credit constrained with a larger number that, on their own account, are not. The literature that finds credit constraints lowering farm productivity identifies the constrained explicitly [@Guirkinger2008; @Kumar2013; @Dessie2015]; the contrast estimated here is a different object, and a negative gap for borrowers against a largely unconstrained comparison group is not in tension with it. If the households that choose not to borrow are, on average, the ones already operating the better technology, the estimated gap partly reflects that sorting. Table 6 offers a partial check. Within households in which the operator applied for a loan, a subgroup in which demand is held constant, the TGR contrast between credit users and applicants whose household did not obtain credit is `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Loan applied", 1), 1)` percentage points, close to the full-sample gap, so the headline gap is not an artefact of comparing applicants with non-applicants; the efficiency contrast in that row is considerably larger than in the full sample and the meta-frontier contrast correspondingly smaller, but the unfunded comparison group is small and is selected by lenders' decisions, so we do not lean on either. Experimental evidence from Ghana approaches the same distinction from the supply side. Offering maize farmers in the north rainfall-index insurance and cash grants in varying combinations, @Karlan2014 find that farm investment responded to the relaxation of the risk constraint and changed little when capital alone was supplied, which places the binding constraint for that population in uninsured risk rather than in liquidity. On that evidence a negative technology gap among borrowers is not in itself surprising, because relaxing a credit constraint need not move a farm's technology when risk is what binds, and the near-absence of cover against production risk documented in Section 3 is part of the environment in which the loans observed here were taken. The experiment does not, however, settle the reading of the contrast estimated here: it supplied capital to farmers who did not have to seek it, in one crop and one region, so it speaks to access where this treatment records use, and it identifies which constraint binds where this design can only describe the households in which borrowing is observed.

The fourth is measurement. Section 4.3 argues that self-reported borrowing under-records small and informal loans, which would place some genuine borrowers in the comparison group and attenuate the contrast toward zero. Attenuation does not generate a negative gap; it makes the estimated gap, if anything, an understatement of the true difference in absolute value. It cannot explain the sign.

What the data cannot do is assign weights to these readings. The GLSS records the purpose of a loan but not what the household did with the liquidity it freed, records that a loan was granted but not why, and records use rather than access. The disaggregations of Section 5.6 narrow the space somewhat, because the technology gap is present in every financial-service subgroup and in nine of the ten regions, the exception being the least agricultural of them, which is difficult to reconcile with a story confined to one lending channel or one agro-ecology. The honest summary is that the negative technology gap is a robust description of Ghanaian borrowing households, not an estimate of what credit does to a farm.

Placed against the Ghanaian literature, the result reconciles rather than contradicts. Positive credit-efficiency associations have been reported for maize producers under programme and input-linked financing [@Martey2019; @AppiahTwumasi2022], no association for rice under bank-linked credit [@Anang2016], modest output effects of input credit [@Iddrisu2018], and financial inclusion more broadly has been linked to smallholder productivity [@Peprah2021]. Those studies observe credit tied to farm inputs, or crops and regions in which such credit predominates, and they compare borrowers and non-borrowers on a single frontier; the estimates here are national in scope, net of matching on observables, and drawn from a population in which little household borrowing is agricultural. The nationally representative decomposition therefore does not show that agricultural credit fails to move farms toward the frontier; it shows that credit as households actually obtain and use it is not associated with best-practice technology and does not raise or lower within-technology efficiency in any robust way. The distinction between agricultural credit and credit in agricultural households is the paper's substantive contribution to that literature.

Table S4 adds covariate detail that points the same way. In the matched metafrontier, whose one-sided term is the technology gap, the gap is larger for female-operated farms (coefficient `r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Female farmer (dummy)", 4), 3)`) and smaller where the household owns its land (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Land owned (dummy)", 4), 3)`), uses mechanized equipment (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Mechanization (dummy)", 4), 3)`), receives extension advice (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Extension (dummy)", 4), 3)`) or grows a more diversified crop mix (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Crop diversification (index)", 4), 3)`), all significant at the 1% level, while years of schooling carries a small positive coefficient (`r fmt_num(tbl_num("tableS4", "Education (years)", 4), 3)`), meaning a larger distance from best practice. Distance from best practice is thus associated with the same tenure, service and gender factors that structure technology access in Ghanaian agriculture generally [@Adaku2023; @Asravor2024], not with the borrowing indicator that defines the groups.

The policy reading follows from which channel carries the gap. A shortfall located in technical efficiency would call for managerial support through extension, training and record-keeping bundled with the loan; the evidence does not support that diagnosis, because the efficiency difference is small, of unstable sign, and disappears once borrowers are compared with similar non-borrowers. A shortfall located in the technology gap calls for changing the technology farms can obtain and use, but here the gap is not the technology gap that input-constrained farms display, because credit users apply fewer purchased inputs rather than more, and it appears alongside loans that are mostly not used on the farm. The finding therefore does not support expanding household credit as such as an instrument for closing Ghana's crop technology gap, and it does not support the opposite proposition either, since the design cannot establish what credit does to a given farm. It is consistent with the view, long argued for agricultural finance in sub-Saharan Africa, that finance moves technology only when it is designed around the farm's investment and timing needs and bundled with the inputs, information and risk instruments that make the investment worth undertaking [@Meyer2015; @Barrett2022], and with demand-side accounts in which low uptake reflects the limited value farmers see in the products on offer [@DeJanvry2020]. The bundling argument is consistent with these findings, but it is not tested by them; Section 6 draws out the implications after the robustness and heterogeneity evidence has been presented.

## 5.5 Robustness of the main findings

Three features of the main result need to survive scrutiny: the sign and size of the TGR gap, the smallness of the TE gap, and the consequent attribution of the MTE gap to technology. Efficiency scores are not specification-free. The inputs entered, the functional form, the distribution assumed for the one-sided term and the estimator used to recover producer-level scores can each move mean efficiency and the ranking of producers within the same data [@VanNguyen2021], so no single specification can establish the size, and still less the sign, of a difference between two groups' scores; the spread of estimates across defensible specifications is itself the evidence, and we read it that way rather than selecting the specification that gives the cleanest answer. We examine each of the three features across the definition of treatment, the matched sample and the frontier specification, and the exercise separates them rather than confirming them together: the technology component holds its sign throughout and its size across everything except the identity of the borrower, while the efficiency component holds neither.

Table 5 varies whose borrowing defines the household as a credit user; each definition is fitted as its own pair of frontiers, so the non-user column varies across rows. The technology gap is negative and significant under three of the four definitions and indistinguishable from zero under the fourth, and the pattern of which is which is informative rather than merely reassuring. It is `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` percentage points under the household definition, `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points when the spouse holds the loan and `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Household members other than spouses or child", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points when another member does, each significant at the 1% level; but under the operator's own credit it is `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Farmer", 3, block = "Technology gap ratio (TGR)")), 1)` points and does not reach conventional significance. The technology gap, in other words, is absent precisely where the borrower and the farmer are the same person, and widest where the loan is held by the spouse. That ordering is difficult to reconcile with any account in which borrowing itself places a household on a poorer technology, and it is what the loan-use reading of Section 5.4 would predict: a loan taken by the operator is the one most likely to reach the farm, and it is the one associated with no technology gap at all. The efficiency component is significant under only two of the four definitions. It is `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Anyone including farmer", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` percentage points in credit users' favour under the household definition and a much larger `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Pure farmer technical efficiency (TE)")), 1)` points in their favour under spousal credit; under the operator-only and other-member definitions it is small and does not reach conventional significance, so no efficiency contrast is established there in either direction. The MTE gap, by contrast, is negative and significant under all four, from `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points under the operator-only definition to `r fmt_num(abs(100 * tbl_num("table5", "Spouse of farmer", 3, block = "Meta-frontier technical efficiency (MTE)")), 1)` points under spousal credit. Overall performance relative to best practice is therefore lower for credit users however the loan-holder is defined, even under the one definition for which neither component reaches significance on its own. Two qualifications belong with this. The narrower definitions rest on far fewer treated observations than the household definition, so their standard errors are correspondingly larger and the operator-only null is an imprecise null rather than a demonstrated zero. And the matched sample is balanced on having household credit, not on who within the household holds it, so these rows compare differently-composed borrower groups against differently-composed comparison groups rather than isolating the identity of the borrower.

Fig. S1 reports covariate balance for the unmatched sample and for each of the eight matched samples described in Section 4.3, on absolute standardized mean differences, variance ratios and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics. The unmatched sample is most imbalanced on schooling, household size and several crop-share, ethnicity and regional indicators. Every matched sample brings the standardized differences and Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistics close to zero on nearly all covariates, the propensity-score and robust Mahalanobis schemes bring the variance ratios closest to one, and the differences among the propensity-score schemes are small, so the choice among them is not consequential for balance; the probit propensity-score sample, which the composite ranking selects, underlies Tables 4 to 6 and Figures 1 to 4. Two covariates deserve mention. Household size is the one covariate on which a standardized difference of moderate size survives in every matched sample, and the propensity-score matches leave a moderate difference in operator age that the distance-based matches remove, so balance on those dimensions is imperfect; given the family-labour result of Section 5.2, this is a further reason not to over-read the small TE gap.

Fig. S2 re-estimates the three gaps under the alternative specifications listed in Section 4.5, with the preferred estimate marked as a reference band. Across the eight matched samples, formed on Euclidean, scaled Euclidean, Mahalanobis and robust Mahalanobis distance and on logit, probit, complementary log-log and cauchit propensity scores, the TGR gap is negative and of similar size in every case, the MTE gap is negative in every case, and the TE gap is positive in every case, ranging from near zero to about two percentage points. The unmatched sample is the single point at which the efficiency gap changes sign: there it is negative and several times larger in magnitude, alongside a larger negative MTE gap and a TGR gap slightly closer to zero than the matched ones. The sign of the efficiency gap is therefore a property of whether the comparison group is balanced rather than of the estimator, which is the lesson of Table 4 restated across eight matching schemes. Computing scores by the Jondrow-type or the conditional-model estimator rather than the Battese-Coelli estimator, and aggregating operator-level scores by the simple mean or the median rather than the weighted mean, leave all three gaps close to the preferred estimate, and none changes sign. Replacing the translog with a Cobb-Douglas frontier leaves the TGR and MTE gaps negative, but the Cobb-Douglas technology gap carries a standard error large enough that it is not distinguishable from zero, so the functional form matters for the precision of that estimate even where it barely moves its location. Lifting the regularity restrictions leaves the TGR gap unchanged to four decimal places and moves only the efficiency margins, the TE gap falling close to zero and the MTE gap becoming somewhat more negative. That the technology component is invariant to the regularity restrictions is a further reason to treat it as the robust finding and the efficiency margin as the fragile one.

The distributional assumption on the one-sided term is where the exercise reaches its limit, and the limit is worth stating plainly rather than summarising away. The frontier is estimated under five distributions for the inefficiency term: the half-normal baseline, the exponential, the truncated skewed Laplace, the generalized exponential and the truncated normal. Three of the five agree closely. The half-normal, exponential and truncated skewed Laplace each give a negative technology gap -- the latter two somewhat larger than the baseline -- with usable jackknife standard errors, together with a small positive efficiency gap and a negative meta-frontier gap. The generalized exponential also gives a negative technology gap, but with a standard error several times the estimate, and it returns a positive meta-frontier gap; nothing can be read from it in either direction. The truncated normal does not estimate at all: it returns a positive technology-gap point estimate with no standard error, and no efficiency or meta-frontier estimate. We draw no inference from those two, and they mark the boundary of the claim rather than a qualification of it. The half-normal is retained as the baseline because it is the specification that estimates on every subsample and every jackknife replicate. The finding that credit users sit farther below the metafrontier is therefore established under three of the five distributions examined, and under every treatment-definition apart from the operator-only case, every functional form, efficiency estimator, aggregation rule, matching scheme and regularity variant; it is not established across all five distributions, and the paper does not claim that it is. Taken together, the robustness exercise ranks the three findings by their stability: the negative technology gap is the most robust, surviving every dimension except the identity of the borrower and the two distributions that fail to estimate; the negative MTE gap is robust in sign and moderately sensitive in magnitude; and the TE gap is small wherever it estimates, positive in every matched sample and negative only without matching, so its sign is a statement about the comparison group rather than about borrowing.

## 5.6 Heterogeneity across financial-service use, farmers, crops and regions

The gaps reported so far average over households that differ in their other financial services, their characteristics, their crops and their locations. This subsection asks where the technology gap and the efficiency gap are concentrated. The disaggregated estimates summarize the operator-level TGR, TE and MTE from the single matched metafrontier within each subgroup; the frontiers are not re-estimated by subgroup, so the estimates describe heterogeneity within the main result rather than separate models, and the same associational reading applies. In Table 6 each cell is the credit-user mean less the non-user mean within the stated group.

Figure 2 and Table 6 examine the contrast across financial-service use, which is where the paper's framing in terms of financial inclusion rather than credit alone is tested; no exhibit reports the decomposition by the financial-inclusion index, which enters the analysis as a matching covariate rather than as a stratifier and whose construction is documented in Note S1. The technology gap is negative and significant within every financial-service subgroup the GLSS allows: `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Has bank account/contributing to a scheme", 1), 1)` percentage points among households with a formal account, `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Insured", 1), 1)` among the insured, and, across institution types, from `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Investment/mortgage", 1), 1)` points among the small group holding an investment or mortgage account to `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Cooperative/credit union", 1), 1)` among cooperative and credit-union members, with bank customers, savings-and-loans participants, susu members and mobile-money users falling between them. There is no financial-service configuration in these data within which borrowing households operate the best-practice technology, and holding another financial product does not narrow the technology gap of credit users.

What the disaggregation does not show is any complementarity between credit and formal account ownership. Figure 2 splits the contrast by whether the household holds a formal account, and the two halves are close to identical: the technology gap is marginally wider among account holders, the efficiency contrast is positive and of essentially the same size in both, and the resulting meta-frontier gaps differ by well under a percentage point. Account ownership neither amplifies nor offsets the credit contrast on either margin. Because the financial-inclusion literature anticipates that credit works better where it sits alongside savings and payment services [@Peprah2021; @DemirgucKunt2017], the absence of any interaction is worth reporting in its own right; it is a null result rather than a reversal, and we report it as one.

Institution type is the one dimension on which the efficiency margin varies appreciably, and it does not resolve into a mechanism. The TE contrast runs against credit users among savings-and-loans participants (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Savings and loans scheme", 2), 1)` points), cooperative and credit-union members (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Cooperative/credit union", 2), 1)`) and customers of commercial, community and rural banks (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Commercial/community/rural bank", 2), 1)`), and in their favour among susu-scheme participants (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Susu scheme", 2), 1)`), mobile-money users (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Mobile money", 2), 1)`) and the investment or mortgage group (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Investment/mortgage", 2), 1)`), for whom the advantage is large enough that credit users outperform matched non-users against the metafrontier by `r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Investment/mortgage", 3), 1)` points. The MTE gap is correspondingly widest among cooperative and credit-union members (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Cooperative/credit union", 3), 1)` points) and savings-and-loans participants (`r fmt_num(100 * tbl_num("table6", "Savings and loans scheme", 3), 1)`). We do not read a mechanism into this ordering. It places the two group-based channels on opposite sides -- susu favourable, cooperatives and credit unions unfavourable -- which no account of peer monitoring or savings discipline predicts, and the subgroups are small and overlapping, since a household may hold several of these products at once. The data cannot say whether these patterns reflect the kind of credit each channel supplies, the kind of household that uses it, or the uses to which the liquidity is put. A decomposition of the credit contrast by the source of the loan and by its reported purpose, the two dimensions Table 3 records and that no current exhibit crosses with the operator-level scores, would test that directly; it is not available here, and we identify it as the cut the evidence most needs rather than anticipate what it would show. The source-of-information block of Table 6 is reported for completeness and not interpreted, because its category labels do not map consistently onto the corresponding block of Table 2 read in Section 3, and the reasons-for-no-account block, whose category indicators rest on the same response-coding mechanism, is likewise left uninterpreted.

Figure 3 disaggregates by operator gender, age and education. The technology gap is negative and significant in every group, so no demographic group of credit users operates a technology closer to best practice than its matched non-users. The gap is wider for female than for male operators, which is consistent with the larger technology gap for female-operated farms in Table S4 and with the gender gaps in technology use documented on the same data [@Adaku2023]; it narrows with operator age; and it is not monotone in schooling, being narrowest for operators with no formal education and wider at every level above it. The efficiency contrast favours credit users in most groups -- more so for women than for men, and diminishing with age until it is indistinguishable from zero among operators aged sixty and over -- but it runs against them in two: operators with junior secondary schooling and, more strongly, the small group educated beyond senior secondary level, for whom credit users are markedly less efficient within their own technology. The MTE gap is negative in every group, narrowest for operators with senior secondary schooling and with no formal education, where the efficiency advantage offsets part of the technology gap, and widest by a considerable margin for the post-secondary group, where the two margins compound. The expectation that better-educated, prime-age male operators would convert credit into technology gains more readily is not borne out; the technology gap is broad-based, and where the credit contrast is least adverse it is because of an efficiency offset rather than a narrower technology gap.

Figure 4 disaggregates by major crop and by administrative region. Across crops the technology gap is negative and significant for nine of the ten crops shown, widest for yam, cassava and maize and narrowest for sorghum and plantain; for cocoa alone it is indistinguishable from zero. There is thus no crop in which credit-using households operate a technology closer to best practice than their matched non-users, and the cocoa case is an absence of difference rather than an advantage. That absence remains consistent with the large cocoa-share coefficient in the credit-user frontier noted in Section 5.2, and cocoa is the one export crop, with sector-specific input and extension arrangements of its own [@Tsiboe2016]; whether it reflects those arrangements or the selection of better-endowed households into cocoa borrowing cannot be established from the survey, which does not record loan purpose by crop. The efficiency contrast is more uniform than it was across the other disaggregations: it favours credit users in every crop, significantly in nine of the ten and negligibly for sorghum. The MTE gap is accordingly negative for every crop except cocoa, widest for millet, groundnut and rice, and close to zero for plantain, where the efficiency advantage is largest and offsets most of a moderate technology gap. Across regions the technology gap is negative and significant in nine of the ten, widest in Volta, Brong Ahafo and Eastern and narrowest in Western and Northern; it is positive in Greater Accra, the only region in which credit users operate a technology closer to best practice and much the least agricultural region in the sample, so that estimate should not be read as a rural finding. The efficiency contrast favours credit users in eight regions, is indistinguishable from zero in Upper East and runs against them only in Western, and the MTE gap is negative in every region except Greater Accra, widest in the two Upper regions. The crop and regional patterns do not sort by agro-ecology or by cash-crop status, since the widest and among the narrowest technology gaps are both in southern regions, and they do not line up with the density of financial services in Table 2, so we do not attempt to attribute them. What they establish is that the technology gap is pervasive rather than concentrated in a few crops or locations, while the efficiency contrast, where it is not zero, runs mildly in credit users' favour -- a combination more consistent with readings that operate through the household, such as loan use and selection, than with one that operates through the lending environment.

For targeting, the heterogeneity results cut two ways. Because the technology gap is negative in nearly every subgroup, there is no identifiable class of borrowers, defined by service use, gender, age, schooling, crop or region, for whom credit use is associated with a technology closer to best practice; cocoa producers and, on the efficiency margin, cooperative and credit-union members are the nearest to exceptions. Where the subgroups differ is in whether credit users make up part of the technology gap through better within-technology performance, as unbanked households, younger and female operators and plantain and groundnut producers do, or compound it, as banked households, the most educated operators and susu participants do. That is a statement about where managerial support would and would not find a deficit to close, and about the fact that the subgroups in which the overall shortfall is largest, account holders and the post-secondary educated, are not those a financial-inclusion programme would ordinarily prioritize; it is not evidence that credit itself works better for some groups than for others.
